steps.title: The big picture
steps.description: A desktop or mobile client fetches channel history through the HTTP API and opens a separate WebSocket session for live events. Both paths depend on message state, with the gateway handling live delivery.

steps.title: Identity, guilds and permissions
steps.description: Authentication establishes identity. Guild membership and role checks authorize channel access; a valid token alone is not permission to read every message.

steps.title: Connections, presence and fanout
steps.description: A WebSocket session receives live state. Guild and fanout processes coordinate online recipients; a TTL cache illustrates ephemeral presence rather than authoritative message history.

steps.title: Persist a message before delivery
steps.description: An HTTP message request reaches the data service and durable storage. A committed message can drive asynchronous delivery. Rust data services and ScyllaDB are publicly documented; this event-delivery boundary is simplified.

steps.title: Independent background consumers
steps.description: Notifications, indexing, moderation and analytics consume events independently in this teaching model. Retry-safe consumers avoid repeating side effects; a slow consumer should not block the interactive request.

steps.title: Attachments and media
steps.description: The client requests an authorized upload path. Media checks and object storage separate large files from message records; the resulting attachment reference can be included in a message.

steps.title: Voice and video use another path
steps.description: Gateway and guild processes handle signaling and voice-server assignment. Media then travels through a voice/video forwarding server; audio packets do not need to traverse the message database.

steps.title: Recover without treating caches as history
steps.description: After reconnecting, the client can request durable history and resume live subscriptions. Cache loss and consumer retries need recovery paths; not every subsystem shares the same availability or consistency requirement.

steps.title: The complete system
steps.description: All introduced components appear together. Connections summarize responsibility boundaries rather than every request, reply or deployment. Discord publishes multiple subsystem designs; this map combines those observations with illustrative supporting services.
